questions.text: Tell me about a time you identified a problem in the inventory process and fixed it.

key_points: Describe how you spotted the gap — data anomaly, cycle count, system vs physical discrepancy
Explain the root cause you identified
Walk through your specific action — process change, system config, team training
Quantify the result: shrinkage %, accuracy rate, time saved
avoid: Blaming the team or predecessor
Vague 'I improved the process' with no numbers

questions.text: Describe a time when a supplier failed to deliver and you had to solve it fast.

key_points: Set the stakes — what would have stopped if you did nothing
Your immediate triage: what info did you need first
How you sourced alternatives or negotiated partial delivery
Communication to internal stakeholders throughout
avoid: Waiting passively for the supplier to respond
Only mentioning the problem, not your actions

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to manage conflicting priorities across multiple stakeholders.

key_points: Name the stakeholders and their conflicting needs
How you assessed which was truly urgent vs important
Communication approach — how you set expectations with each party
Outcome and what you would do differently
avoid: Saying you 'just worked harder'
Leaving one stakeholder in the dark

questions.text: Describe a time you used data to change a decision that was already in motion.

key_points: What decision was being made and by whom
What data you found that contradicted the current direction
How you presented it — to whom, in what format
Result: was the decision changed? What was the impact?
avoid: Generic 'I like data-driven decisions'
Claiming credit for the whole outcome

questions.text: Tell me about a time you led a cross-functional project with supply chain at its core.

key_points: Scope of project and which functions were involved
Your specific role — did you have formal authority or not
How you aligned different teams with different incentives
Delivery outcome and lessons learned
avoid: Describing a single-team project as cross-functional
Not mentioning how you handled disagreements

questions.text: Walk me through how you build a demand forecast from scratch for a new product.

key_points: Identify analogous products and use their history as baseline
Gather market data: launch promotions, distribution plan, seasonal patterns
Use qualitative input: sales team, marketing, customer commitments
Set initial safety stock higher to absorb uncertainty, reduce as actuals come in
Establish a review cadence — weekly for first 90 days
avoid: 'I'd just use historical data' — there is none for new products
Not mentioning forecast error measurement

questions.text: What forecasting methods have you used and when would you choose one over another?

key_points: Moving average: simple, works for stable demand with no trend
Exponential smoothing: weights recent data more, good for trends
ARIMA: handles seasonality and autocorrelation, needs clean history
ML models: high-volume SKUs with rich feature data
Causal models: when external drivers (promotions, weather) strongly influence demand
strong_answer_signals: knows when NOT to use complex models
avoid: Only naming methods without explaining trade-offs
Claiming ML is always better

questions.text: How do you calculate reorder point and safety stock? Walk me through your approach.

key_points: Reorder Point = (Average daily demand × Lead time) + Safety stock
Safety stock = Z-score × σ(demand) × √Lead time — for service level target
Factors that change it: lead time variability, demand variability, service level target
ABC classification to apply different service level targets by SKU importance
Review cycle: how often do you recalculate as actuals change?
avoid: Giving formula without context
Not mentioning lead time variability as a key driver

questions.text: What is ABC analysis and how have you used it in inventory management?

key_points: A items: ~20% of SKUs, ~80% of value — tight control, frequent counts
B items: moderate value — standard controls
C items: high quantity, low value — bulk ordering, less frequent review
Can extend to XYZ for demand variability (X=stable, Z=erratic)
Practical use: cycle count frequency, service level targets, reorder strategy
strong_answer_signals: links ABC to actual policy differences
used it to reduce counting labor
avoid: Only defining it without a practical example of how you used it

questions.text: Describe your experience with S&OP. What was your role and what made it effective or ineffective?

key_points: S&OP steps: demand review → supply review → pre-S&OP → executive S&OP
Your specific role: data preparation, facilitation, or decision-making
What worked: clear ownership, standardized data, pre-reads circulated in advance
What didn't: siloed inputs, HiPPO decisions overriding data, no action tracking
strong_answer_signals: can critique the process not just describe it
avoid: Describing it as just a monthly meeting
Not mentioning the balance between supply and demand

questions.text: How do you measure forecast accuracy and what do you do when it consistently misses?

key_points: MAPE: mean absolute percentage error — good for comparison across SKUs
WMAPE: weighted by revenue — avoids low-volume SKU noise
Bias: are you consistently over or under forecasting?
Root cause analysis: new competitor, promo not captured, seasonality shift
Corrective actions: model recalibration, adding causal variables, consensus adjustment
strong_answer_signals: knows the difference between MAPE and bias
mentions acting on bias separately from error
avoid: Only citing MAPE without bias tracking
No clear action when accuracy is poor

questions.text: What ERP or planning tools have you worked with? How deeply did you use them?

key_points: Name specific systems: SAP (MM/PP/APO), Oracle, Microsoft D365, Blue Yonder, Kinaxis, o9
Distinguish between user vs configurator vs implementer
Specific modules: MRP run, safety stock planning, transportation management
Any custom reporting or integration work you contributed to
strong_answer_signals: specific module names not just system names
avoid: Listing tools without explaining how you used them
Overstating experience — interviewers probe deeply

questions.text: How would you reduce inventory carrying cost without increasing stockout risk?

key_points: Improve forecast accuracy → reduce safety stock needed
Reduce lead time variability through supplier collaboration
Implement vendor-managed inventory (VMI) for C-items
Review min/max and reorder points — many are set and forgotten
Consignment stock for slow-moving high-value items
strong_answer_signals: quantifies the carrying cost % they targeted
mentions supplier collaboration not just internal levers
avoid: Just saying 'order less' — misses the service level trade-off
Not addressing the stockout risk explicitly

questions.text: Walk me through how you would implement a new demand planning system.

key_points: Discovery: current state pain points, data availability, integration landscape
Requirements: user stories from planners, finance, sales
Data readiness: cleanliness, history length, master data governance
Pilot: one product family, one region first — measure before scaling
Change management: training, champion network, parallel run period
strong_answer_signals: data readiness first — most implementations fail here
change management is not an afterthought
avoid: Going straight to vendor selection
Not mentioning data quality as a blocker

questions.text: What is the bullwhip effect and how have you dealt with it?

key_points: Demand variability amplifies upstream: retailer orders > wholesaler orders > manufacturer orders
Causes: batch ordering, price fluctuations, shortage gaming, forecast errors
Mitigations: share POS data directly with suppliers, reduce order batching
Vendor-managed inventory reduces information distortion
Shorter replenishment cycles, better visibility across the chain
strong_answer_signals: has a practical example of reducing it
mentions information sharing as the core fix
avoid: Only defining it from a textbook
Not connecting it to practical supply chain tools

questions.text: You have three high-priority replenishment orders due today and only enough resource to complete two. What do you do?

key_points: Triage by impact: which stockout causes the most business damage
Check if any can be partially fulfilled to buy time
Communicate immediately — do not let the miss be a surprise
Escalate if the trade-off is above your authority
Document the decision and rationale
strong_answer_signals: proactive communication before the miss happens
avoid: Just 'working harder to do all three'
Making the call silently without informing stakeholders

questions.text: Your forecast model has been accurate for two years. Suddenly it's missing badly. What's your process?

key_points: First: is the data input correct? Check for feed errors or master data changes
Look at bias direction — consistently over or under?
Segment by product, region, channel — where is the miss concentrated?
External drivers: competitor entry, economic shift, channel mix change
Short-term: override manually with judgment; long-term: recalibrate model
strong_answer_signals: separates short-term fix from long-term fix
avoid: Immediately blaming the model
Making a global model change based on a few data points

questions.text: Sales is pushing you to increase forecast by 30% for next quarter to support a key customer deal. Finance says hold the line. What do you do?

key_points: Ask sales for the specifics: committed PO or optimistic projection?
Model two scenarios: base case and upside case — show the inventory risk of each
Present the financial cost of being wrong in both directions
Recommend a consensus position with a trigger point to act on the upside
Get alignment in writing before committing supply
strong_answer_signals: scenario modeling not just one answer
gets specifics from sales before deciding
avoid: Just picking one side
Agreeing without understanding the source of the 30%

questions.text: You discover a warehouse discrepancy: the system shows 500 units but a physical count found 320. What are your next steps?

key_points: Recount first — rule out counting error
Check recent transactions: receipts, shipments, transfers, adjustments
Look for timing issues: in-transit not yet received, goods in quarantine
If confirmed: write-off or adjustment with approval, update system
Root cause: is this a one-time event or a systemic process gap?
strong_answer_signals: asks why not just fixes the number
avoid: Immediately adjusting the system without investigating
Not flagging to management

questions.text: You're asked to cut inventory by 20% in 90 days. How do you approach this without damaging service levels?

key_points: Baseline analysis: where does the current inventory sit? Which SKUs are slow/excess?
Quick wins: liquidate obsolete stock, cancel open POs where possible
Demand signal review: are min/max parameters still correct?
Supplier negotiations: reduce order quantities, increase frequency
Monitor service level weekly — stop reduction if fill rate degrades
strong_answer_signals: starts with data not with targets
has a monitoring mechanism with a stop rule
avoid: Cutting uniformly across all SKUs
Not tracking service level impact during the process

questions.text: Why do you want to move from operations into demand planning?

key_points: Bridge what you've done to what you want: operations gave you ground-level insight into supply variability
Express what pulls you toward planning: the analytical, strategic, cross-functional nature
Name a specific moment that crystallized the transition for you
Show preparation: certifications, tools learned, courses taken
strong_answer_signals: specific moment or insight, not vague desire
connects past experience as an asset not a liability
avoid: 'I want a desk job'
Implying operations was just a stepping stone you tolerated

questions.text: What does good supply chain performance look like to you?

key_points: Balance: service level (fill rate, OTIF) alongside cost (inventory turns, carrying cost)
Visibility: knowing what's happening before it becomes a problem
Resilience: can the chain absorb disruption without catastrophic failure
Collaboration: internal alignment between sales, ops, finance — not siloed optimization
strong_answer_signals: mentions both service AND cost — not just one
talks about resilience not just efficiency
avoid: Only mentioning cost reduction
Abstract answer with no specific metrics

questions.text: What's the most complex supply chain problem you've worked on, and why did it matter?

key_points: Choose a problem with real stakes — revenue, service, or cost impact
Explain why it was complex: multiple variables, stakeholders, or unknowns
Walk through your approach — not just what you did but how you thought
Quantify the outcome and reflect on what you'd do differently
strong_answer_signals: shows systems thinking not just task execution
avoid: Choosing a simple problem and over-dramatizing it
Not quantifying the impact

questions.text: How do you build a demand planning team's capability when you inherit planners with varying skill levels?

key_points: Start with a skills assessment: technical (tools, stats), process, and judgment
Pair stronger planners with developing ones on rotations or shadow reviews
Create a standard operating model: templates, review cadence, escalation rules
Invest in training: APICS, IBF certification, internal workshops
Measure and celebrate accuracy improvements to build culture of ownership
strong_answer_signals: peer learning not just top-down training
avoid: Replacing the team immediately
Only sending people to courses without structural change

questions.text: How do you get executive buy-in for a supply chain technology investment?

key_points: Quantify the current cost: excess inventory, expediting, stockouts, planner time
Model the ROI: conservative, base, and upside scenario
Address risk: implementation risk, change management, data readiness
Find an internal champion in finance or operations
Propose a pilot first — reduces commitment anxiety
strong_answer_signals: pilot strategy to reduce perceived risk
avoid: Leading with features of the technology
Not having a finance-aligned business case

questions.text: Describe how you've managed the tension between sales optimism and supply chain realism in forecasting.

key_points: Establish a structured consensus process — not a negotiation, a data review
Show sales the cost of over-forecasting: write-offs, working capital tied up
Create shared accountability: if sales commits to a number, they own it
Track and publish forecast accuracy by input source — transparency reduces gaming
Build the relationship outside the forecast meeting — trust reduces politics
strong_answer_signals: uses data to depoliticize the conversation
avoid: Framing it as supply chain vs sales
Letting sales override without consequence or tracking

questions.text: Tell me about a time you improved a KPI that had been stuck for a long time.

key_points: Name the KPI and why it had been difficult to move
Describe your diagnostic approach — what had been tried before
Explain your specific intervention and why it was different
Quantify the improvement and how long it held
strong_answer_signals: sustainable improvement not a one-time fix
avoid: Vague 'I improved efficiency'
Not explaining why it had been stuck

questions.text: Describe a time you had to learn a new system or tool quickly under pressure.

key_points: What was the system and the deadline
Your learning approach: documentation, peer help, trial and error
How you ensured accuracy while still learning
What you'd do differently with more time
avoid: Implying you struggled so much the work suffered
Not showing any initiative

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to push back on a request from a senior leader.

key_points: What was being asked and why it was problematic
How you prepared your case — data, alternatives, risk framing
How you delivered the pushback — timing, tone, setting
The outcome and what you learned about managing upward
strong_answer_signals: came with alternatives not just objections
avoid: Framing it as 'I was right, they were wrong'
Never having pushed back — raises a red flag

questions.text: Give an example of when you caught an error before it became a costly problem.

key_points: What type of error: data entry, system, process, forecast
How you caught it — routine check, anomaly detection, gut instinct confirmed by data
What would have happened if uncaught — quantify the risk
What process change you put in place to prevent recurrence
avoid: Trivial errors that had minimal impact
No follow-up prevention step

questions.text: Describe a time you worked with a difficult colleague to get a supply chain project across the line.

key_points: Describe the difficulty specifically — different priorities, communication style, or conflict of interest
How you adjusted your approach to work with them
What compromises or trade-offs were made
Outcome and whether the relationship improved
avoid: Making the colleague sound incompetent
Claiming there was no difficulty

questions.text: What is OTIF and how do you improve it when it's consistently below target?

key_points: OTIF = On Time In Full — % of orders delivered complete and on schedule
Decompose: is the issue On Time, In Full, or both? They have different root causes
On Time failures: lead time miscalculation, carrier issues, production delays
In Full failures: inventory shortage, picking errors, supplier partial shipments
Fix cycle: measure by SKU, lane, and carrier — address the biggest buckets first
strong_answer_signals: separates OT from IF root causes
measures at granular level not just total
tracks carrier and supplier performance separately
avoid: Treating OTIF as one undifferentiated metric
Focusing only on internal fixes when carrier or supplier is the issue

questions.text: Explain the difference between MRP and MPS. When would you use each?

key_points: MPS (Master Production Schedule): what finished goods to produce and when — driven by demand forecast and orders
MRP (Material Requirements Planning): what components and raw materials are needed to support the MPS
MPS is the input; MRP is the explosion downstream
MPS is used by planning and sales; MRP is used by procurement and production
Both feed from the demand plan but operate at different levels of the BOM
strong_answer_signals: can explain the BOM explosion logic
ties both back to demand plan
avoid: Confusing them or treating them as interchangeable

questions.text: How do you handle seasonality in your demand forecasting?

key_points: Seasonal index: calculate ratio of period demand to average demand across the year
Apply the index to the baseline trend to get the seasonal forecast
Use at least 2-3 years of history to smooth out anomalous seasons
Adjust for known changes: new store openings, discontinued promotions
Flag and quarantine COVID or other extreme outlier years before calculating indices
strong_answer_signals: knows how to calculate the index
adjusts for structural changes not just pattern-matching
avoid: Just saying 'I use the same period last year'
Not accounting for year-over-year structural changes

questions.text: What is Days on Hand (DOH) and how do you use it to manage inventory health?

key_points: DOH = (Inventory on Hand / Average Daily Demand)
Tells you how many days of supply you're holding at current consumption rate
Use to identify excess: if DOH >> your target cycle stock + safety stock
Segment: track separately by SKU class, not just in aggregate
Set targets by category: fast movers vs slow movers require different DOH targets
strong_answer_signals: links DOH to carrying cost explicitly
sets different targets by SKU class
uses it proactively not just for reporting
avoid: Treating a single DOH target as right for all SKUs

questions.text: How do you handle slow-moving and obsolete (SLOB) inventory?

key_points: Definition: slow-moving = below X turns/year; obsolete = end-of-life or superseded
Identification: run regular aging reports — flag items with no movement > 90/180 days
Disposition options: liquidation, return to supplier, donation, redeployment, write-off
Prevention: better new product launch forecasting, min order quantity negotiation, shorter replenishment cycles
Finance partnership: provision early to avoid year-end surprises
strong_answer_signals: mentions prevention not just reactive management
avoid: Only talking about writing it off
No mention of prevention

questions.text: Walk me through how you would design a Sales & Operations Planning process from scratch.

key_points: Step 1: Data review — statistical baseline, actuals vs forecast, inventory position
Step 2: Demand review — sales and marketing input, assumptions documented
Step 3: Supply review — capacity, supplier constraints, production plan
Step 4: Pre-S&OP — align finance, resolve gaps, escalate unresolved issues
Step 5: Executive S&OP — decision-making, investment calls, strategic alignment
Key success factors: pre-reads sent 48h in advance, decisions logged, action tracker maintained
avoid: Describing it as just a monthly meeting
Not mentioning finance integration

questions.text: How do you manage a multi-echelon inventory network?

key_points: Multi-echelon: central DC → regional DC → store/customer — each level holds stock
Challenge: optimizing total system inventory, not just each node in isolation
Key principle: safety stock should be held at the right echelon based on lead time and variability
Techniques: inventory positioning analysis, postponement strategy, lateral transshipment
Tools: multi-echelon optimization software (e.g., Llamasoft, ToolsGroup, Blue Yonder)
avoid: Treating each node as independent
Not mentioning the trade-off between holding cost and service level at each echelon

questions.text: A key raw material is facing a global shortage. You have 6 weeks of supply. What do you do right now?

key_points: Immediate: lock in any available supply — buy forward if economics allow
Triage demand: which customers or products are highest priority?
Explore substitutes: engineering or procurement review of alternative materials
Communicate: sales, operations, and leadership need to know now — not when stock runs out
Build a daily tracker: supply remaining, consumption rate, projected stockout date
strong_answer_signals: acts immediately not after more analysis
avoid: Waiting for the situation to clarify before acting
Only focusing on procurement without rationing demand

questions.text: Your top customer suddenly doubles their order with two weeks notice. How do you respond?

key_points: First: check actual available inventory and open POs
Can you expedite inbound supply? At what cost?
Check production or warehouse capacity constraints
Commercial check: is this firm demand or a hedge? Get commitment in writing
If you can't fulfill fully: partial shipment plan with clear timeline, communicated proactively
strong_answer_signals: proactive partial fulfillment plan if constrained
avoid: Saying yes before checking feasibility
Surprising the customer with a shortfall at delivery

questions.text: Finance wants you to hit an inventory reduction target that you believe will cause stockouts in Q4, your peak season. How do you handle it?

key_points: Build the model: project service level at the proposed inventory level using historical demand variability
Quantify the revenue at risk from stockouts — in dollars finance understands
Present two scenarios: hit the target and risk X in lost sales vs hold inventory and carry Y in cost
Propose an alternative: reduce non-peak items, not peak-season critical SKUs
Escalate with a recommendation, not just a problem
strong_answer_signals: quantifies stockout risk in revenue terms
escalates with data not just instinct
avoid: Just complaining that the target is unrealistic
Not quantifying the risk

questions.text: You join a new company and find the demand planning process is entirely manual in Excel. What's your 90-day plan?

key_points: Days 1-30: listen and learn — understand why it's manual, what pain points exist, where the data lives
Days 31-60: quick wins — standardize the Excel model, document the process, fix obvious data quality issues
Days 60-90: build the business case for a planning tool — quantify planner time, error rate, missed signals
Don't implement a system in 90 days — earn trust first, fix the data, then automate
avoid: Announcing a new system on week two
Dismissing the existing process before understanding it

questions.text: What do you think is the biggest challenge in supply chain planning today?

key_points: Demand volatility: post-pandemic demand patterns are harder to model
Supply chain visibility: most companies still can't see past tier-1 suppliers
Data quality: planning tools are only as good as the master data feeding them
Talent: demand planning is still under-valued and under-staffed vs its business impact
Technology adoption: gap between what tools can do and what companies actually use
strong_answer_signals: has a genuine point of view not a textbook answer
ties the challenge to their own experience
avoid: 'AI and automation' as a generic answer without substance
Not connecting the challenge to practical implications

questions.text: What certifications or learning have you done to develop in supply chain?

key_points: Name certifications: CPIM (ASCM), CSCP, CLTD, IBF CPF, PMP if project-heavy
Self-directed learning: books (Bowersox, Hopp & Spearman), courses, podcasts
On-the-job stretch: took on a project outside your scope to learn something new
Communities: CSCMP, ISM, local supply chain groups
strong_answer_signals: shows self-investment not just employer-funded training
connects learning to specific skill gaps
ongoing not just a historical list
avoid: Only listing employer-mandated training
No evidence of self-directed development

questions.text: How do you measure and improve your demand planning team's performance?

key_points: Team KPIs: WMAPE by planner, forecast bias, on-time completion of planning cycle
Individual development: skill matrix updated quarterly, training tied to gaps
Review cadence: weekly accuracy review, monthly retrospective on biggest misses
Recognition: celebrate when a difficult forecast was accurate — not just when it was easy
Accountability: if a planner's number is consistently off, diagnose together before judging
strong_answer_signals: distinguishes team metrics from individual metrics
development is systematic not ad hoc
avoid: Only measuring accuracy without measuring effort or process quality
No development component

questions.text: Describe how you've driven adoption of a new planning process or tool across a resistant team.

key_points: Understand the resistance first: fear of job loss, distrust of the tool, extra workload perception
Find early adopters — get them results first, let them be advocates
Show the 'what's in it for me': less firefighting, more strategic work, better data
Train in small groups with real data, not generic demos
Track adoption metrics and celebrate progress publicly
strong_answer_signals: diagnoses resistance before responding to it
uses peer influence not just authority
avoid: Mandating use without addressing the why
One big training event and hoping for adoption
